papers.title: Evaluating multivariable clinical prediction models for Parkinson's disease prognosis: A scoping review.
papers.abstract: Multivariable clinical prediction models combine two or more patient predictor variables to calculate the probability of a clinical outcome. In persons with Parkinson's disease (PD), clinical prognostic models can be used to predict disease progression or the occurrence of a clinical event. These models can aid in PD prognostication and complement clinical judgment by informing medical decision-making and resource allocation. In this scoping review of the literature from inception through May 2025, we present data from 74 multivariable prognostic models in PD, organized by clinical outcome. We also describe model development, validation, and calibration, if performed, and identify knowledge gaps. By summarizing existing multivariable clinical prognostic models in PD, this review is designed to inform prognostication and foster the development of more accurate, validated prognostic models for use in clinical practice.

papers.title: Acupuncture is associated with lower accidental injury risk among patients with Parkinson's disease: a nationwide retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) have a high risk of accidental injuries because motor and non-motor symptoms can impair gait, balance, cognition, and autonomic function. Acupuncture has been reported to improve gait and balance, but its association with long-term injury prevention in PD remains unclear. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study using Taiwan's National Health Insurance Research Database. Patients newly diagnosed with PD between 2001 and 2012 were followed through 2018. Propensity score matching (PSM) was used to improve comparability between patients who received acupuncture and those who did not. The PSM cohort was designated as the primary analysis, and a multivariable analysis of the full cohort was supportive. Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: Among 24,467 patients with PD, 7,830 (32.0%) received acupuncture. Accidental injuries occurred in 15.2% of patients in the acupuncture group and 17.1% of patients in the non-acupuncture group. In the primary PSM analysis, acupuncture was associated with a lower risk of hospitalization for accidental injury (aHR, 0.67; 95% CI, 0.42-0.85). The association was strongest for accidental falls, although no simple dose-response relationship was observed across acupuncture-session categories. The supportive full-cohort analysis yielded a similar direction of association (aHR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.39-0.76). CONCLUSION: In this nationwide claims-based cohort, acupuncture use was associated with a lower risk of hospitalization for accidental injury among patients newly diagnosed with PD. Because residual confounding and differences in care-seeking may remain, prospective studies with clinical measures of PD severity are warranted.

papers.title: Epigenetic processes in Parkinson disease.
papers.abstract: Numerous investigations performed over the last 20 years revealed various epigenetic modifications in both postmortem brain samples and in peripheral tissues of individuals with Parkinson disease (PD), as well as in neuronal and animal models of the disease. These include changes in DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation, histone-tail modifications, and a dysregulated expression of both short- and long-noncoding RNA molecules. Overall, there is no doubt that epigenetic modifications occur within the neurodegenerative process linked to PD, resulting in altered expression of PD-linked genes. However, it is not yet completely clear which of these epigenetic changes are a consequence of the neurodegenerative process and which are instead early events capable of contributing to it. Indeed, studies in peripheral tissues of patients at different disease stages are attempting to provide early epigenetic biomarkers of clinical utility. Similarly, the epigenetic properties of ascertained PD risk factors, including metals, herbicides, and pesticides, are being tested in animal and cell culture models to detect environmentally induced epigenetic changes potentially contributing to the disease. The potential of epigenetic treatments and epigenome editing for PD is another area of active research.

papers.title: The gut-brain axis in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases: a comparative perspective.
papers.abstract: Global health challenges associated with neurodegenerative disorders are increasing, prompting growing interest in the gut-brain axis (GBA) as a key contributor to disease pathogenesis. The GBA represents a bidirectional communication network linking the gut microbiota, immune signalling pathways, metabolic processes, and the central nervous system (CNS). This review highlights the role of the GBA in the onset and progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), focusing on comparative disease mechanisms involving microbial dysbiosis, neuroinflammation, and metabolic dysfunction. Particular emphasis is placed on alterations in short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), lipopolysaccharide (LPS), microbial amyloids, and inflammatory mediators including tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), interleukin 1 beta (IL-1β), interleukin 6 (IL-6), toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), and NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome, which contribute to protein misfolding, blood-brain barrier disruption, and the accumulation of amyloid-β, hyperphosphorylated Tau, and α-synuclein. Furthermore, the review discusses recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for integrating microbiome, clinical, neuroimaging, and multi-omics datasets to improve disease prediction, biomarker discovery, and patient stratification. AI approaches, including random forest, support vector machine, convolutional neural networks, and XGBoost, together with microbiome analysis platforms such as QIIME 2 and multi-omics integration tools including mixOmics and MOFA+, are highlighted for their potential in precision neurology. Collectively, integrating GBA biology with AI-driven analytics provides promising opportunities for early diagnosis, personalised therapeutic strategies, and precision medicine to address the growing burden of neurodegenerative disorders.

papers.title: Natural Bioactives Targeting α- Synuclein Aggregation in PD: A Review of Multi-mechanism Phytochemicals.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by the misfolding and aggregation of α-synuclein, a central pathological event that contributes to oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired proteostasis, neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction and progressive dopaminergic neuronal loss. This review highlights current research on natural bioactive compounds that target α-synuclein aggregation as potential disease-modifying therapies for PD. Relevant material was identified through searches of major scientific databases, including PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus and Web of Science, focused on research studying natural products and α-synuclein-associated neurodegeneration. The review examines significant types of phytochemicals, including flavonoids, polyphenols, alkaloids, terpenoids, and related natural substances such as baicalein, Epigallocatechin-3-Gallate (EGCG), berberine, curcumin, naringenin, mangiferin, silibinin, and oleuropein etc. Together, these substances have shown a variety of neuroprotective mechanisms in preclinical models such as preventing α-synuclein fibrillization, improving protein clearance pathways, reducing oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, maintaining mitochondrial function, and modifying cellular signalling pathways related to neuronal survival. Important translational obstacles are also highlighted by the current data, such as low oral bioavailability, quick metabolic breakdown, inadequate brain exposure, and the lack of clinical efficacy for several prospective candidates. Most of the information currently available comes from preclinical trials, even though natural bioactive substances constitute a potential avenue of investigation for targeting α- synuclein disease. papers.title: Resting-state cortical alpha frequency in Parkinson's disease and multiple system atrophy: associations with diagnosis, age, and symptom burden.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are clinically overlapping neurodegenerative disorders that present with a complex, heterogeneous burden of motor and non-motor symptoms. Resting-state EEG reveals that cortical alpha slowing is a hallmark of pathological aging, yet its specific presence and clinical significance in these distinct synucleinopathies remain incompletely understood. Therefore, precisely quantifying the individual alpha frequency serves as a critical, non-invasive approach to characterize cortical network dysfunction across synucleinopathies and evaluate how aging moderates its association with clinical symptom burden. METHODS: We analyzed source-reconstructed resting-state EEG data from 104 participants, comprising patients with PD, patients with the parkinsonian (MSA-P) and cerebellar subtypes (MSA-C) of MSA, and healthy controls. To accurately capture oscillatory dynamics, a data-driven masking empirical mode decomposition approach was applied to extract the individual alpha frequency across canonical cortical networks. General linear models tested diagnostic group differences, age-related effects, and age-dependent associations between individual alpha frequency and clinical symptom scores. RESULTS: Relative to healthy controls, both PD and MSA-C exhibited significant lower cortical IAF, whereas MSA-P showed no significant global IAF difference. At the network level, significant reduction of IAF was detected in the visual and dorsal attention networks in both PD and MSA-C. Advancing age independently contributed to alpha slowing across all participants without accelerating the disease-related trajectories. Notably, chronological age significantly moderated the relationship between alpha slowing and non-motor symptoms. papers.title: Studies on topological maturation of α-synuclein fibrils in Parkinson's disease: Insights from persistent homology and SARS-CoV-2 acceleration of aggregation.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is marked by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and the accumulation of α-synuclein (α-syn) into amyloid fibrils and Lewy bodies. These aggregates impair synaptic function, disrupt proteostasis, compromise mitochondrial health, and drive neuroinflammation and oxidative stress. Clinical observations during the COVID-19 pandemic revealed accelerated motor deterioration and higher mortality among PD patients following SARS-CoV-2 infection, pointing to potential overlapping mechanisms with Alzheimer's disease, including protein misfolding, chronic inflammation, and oxidative damage. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to investigate how the SARS-CoV-2 N-protein may accelerate α-syn aggregation using computational approaches. METHODS: We employed a multimodal, label-free computational pipeline inspired by TopoBind to examine the topological maturation of patient-derived α-syn fibrils across preclinical (PDB 7V47, 8H03), mid-stage (7XO0, 7XO1), and late-stage (8H04, 7V48) PD phases. Per-residue features were extracted using 640-dimensional evolutionary scale modeling (ESM)-2 embeddings, solvent-accessible surface area, and persistent homology based on Vietoris-Rips filtration of Cα coordinates (r = 0-20 Å, persistence threshold > 0.8 Å). Predictions were validated using PyRosetta InterfaceAnalyzerMover, PRODIGY (ΔG and Kd), and normal mode analysis. RESULTS: The pipeline successfully identified key protein-protein interface residues on α-syn fibrils, achieving 74-92% overlap with PyRosetta results. Conserved interaction hotspots were located primarily in the non-amyloid component region, protofilament interfaces, and hydrophobic grooves. papers.title: Minocycline-Mediated Inhibition of Microglial Activation in Neuroinflammation-Related Neuropsychiatric Disorders: Preclinical Promise and Clinical Limitations.
papers.abstract: Minocycline, a second-generation tetracycline antibiotic, has attracted interest as a CNS-active anti-inflammatory agent because it crosses the blood-brain barrier and inhibits microglial activation. This review summarizes preclinical and clinical evidence for minocycline in neuroinflammation-related neuropsychiatric disorders, focusing on Alzheimer's disease (AD), Lewy body disease (LBD), schizophrenia, and major depressive disorder (MDD). Across these disorders, preclinical studies have generally shown that minocycline attenuates microglial activation or maladaptive microglial responses and improves disease-relevant behavioral, synaptic, or neuropathological outcomes. However, clinical translation has been inconsistent. Clinical trials in AD, related parkinsonian disorders, schizophrenia, and MDD have failed to demonstrate robust and reproducible efficacy, despite encouraging preclinical findings. Moreover, direct clinical evidence that minocycline suppresses microglial activation in the human brain remains very limited. These discrepancies between preclinical findings and clinical evidence may reflect heterogeneity in disease stage and microglial states, suboptimal timing of intervention, lack of direct evidence that minocycline suppresses microglial activation in the human brain, and its non-selective anti-inflammatory actions. Future studies should incorporate biomarker-based patient stratification and direct measures of central microglial target engagement.

papers.title: Exploring the potential of resveratrol-enriched cord mesenchymal stem cell derived exosomes in an in vitro Parkinson's model.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and the pathological aggregation of α-synuclein (α-syn) into Lewy bodies and it is known as the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder. The pathogenesis of PD involves mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired protein degradation, and neuroinflammation. Current therapeutic strategies are largely symptomatic and remain limited in their ability to halt disease progression. Resveratrol (Res) has been shown to mitigate oxidative stress, preserve mitochondrial integrity, and reduce α-syn aggregation in PD models due to its antioxidant and neuroprotective properties. Despite its promising therapeutic potential, its poor bioavailability and rapid metabolism hinder the achievement of the desired therapeutic effects, which calls for advanced drug delivery systems. Human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cell (hUC-MSC) exosomes (Exos) are nanoscale extracellular vesicles with intrinsic neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory, and regenerative properties. They represent a promising carrier system owing to biocompatibility and the ability to cross the blood-brain barrier. Since the isolation technique is a critical parameter affecting both Exos yield and therapeutic efficacy, the study initially focused on optimizing the isolation process through a comparative investigation of ultracentrifugation and commercial isolation kits. Exos obtained with the highest yield and optimal characteristics, were subsequently subjected to Res loading through the probe sonication method. After the physicochemical characterization of Res-loaded exosomes (Exo-Res), their therapeutic potential was evaluated in an in vitro PD model established by rotenone-induced neurotoxicity in SH-SY5Y cells. papers.title: Automated eye-tracking for Parkinson's disease diagnosis: a proof-of-concept cascade classifier study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder of increasing prevalence, with diagnostic accuracy of approximately 26% in early symptomatic patients. There is a need for accurate, non-invasive biomarkers to aid in disease diagnosis. METHODS: This proof-of-concept study enrolled 90 participants (PD n RESULTS: Level 1 achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.818 (95% CI: 0.71, 0.91), with a sensitivity of 83% and specificity of 63%. Level 2 achieved an AUC of 0.670 (95% CI: 0.52, 0.80), with a sensitivity of 68% and specificity of 63%. As a proof-of-concept study, the observed performance positions the device as an adjunctive screening tool. Diagnostic discrimination can only be achieved through a much larger Phase III study. Five adverse events were recorded (three cases of dizziness, one of nausea, and one of dry eyes); one participant withdrew from the study. CONCLUSIONS: Preliminary evidence supports clinical validity pending confirmatory Phase III study: reproducible eye-tracking signal for PD is detectable using a two-level cascade classifier. A multi-center confirmatory study is warranted before assessment of clinical utility.Trial registration. ClinicalTrials.govNCT04925622.

papers.title: Targeting Ferroptosis in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Therapeutic Potential and Mechanistic Insights of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs), including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and multiple sclerosis, are characterized by progressive and irreversible neuronal loss, whereas current treatments remain largely symptomatic. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death whose execution is defined by iron-enabled phospholipid peroxidation and failure of cellular ferroptosis-defense systems. Mitochondrial metabolism can modify ferroptosis susceptibility, but its contribution varies with cell type and initiating stimulus. Converging evidence implicates ferroptosis in multiple NDs, in which affected regions commonly show iron accumulation, glutathione depletion, and increased lipid peroxidation. With their multi-component and multi-target properties, traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) interventions may modulate several nodes in this network. This review summarizes the core execution and defense mechanisms of ferroptosis, evaluates their roles in major NDs, and critically appraises bioactive herbal compounds, compound formulas, acupuncture, electroacupuncture, and moxibustion. The reported interventions mainly engage the Nrf2/GPX4 antioxidant axis, TFR1/FPN1/FTH1/NCOA4-mediated iron handling, ACSL4-dependent lipid peroxidation, and GPX4-independent defense systems. Because most studies are preclinical and many infer ferroptosis from non-specific markers, the evidence is graded here as direct, supportive, indirect, mixed, or complementary. Translation will require standardized formulations, causal ferroptosis validation, pharmacokinetic and brain-exposure data, validated human biomarkers, and rigorously designed clinical trials.

papers.title: Cuproptosis: New Mechanisms Linking Endothelial Dysfunction to Neurodegenerative Diseases and Therapeutic Prospects.
papers.abstract: Cuproptosis is a copper-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by disrupted copper homeostasis and mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming. It is distinct from other cell death pathways and has been increasingly linked to vascular endothelial dysfunction and neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. This article comprehensively reviews the core molecular mechanisms of cuproptosis and its emerging roles in endothelial dysfunction and neurodegeneration, synthesizing recent findings from cellular, animal, and human studies. Cuproptosis exacerbates vascular pathology by impairing endothelial barrier function, inducing oxidative stress, and promoting inflammation and senescence. In the brain, it drives neurodegeneration both directly-via mitochondrial damage and neuronal loss-and indirectly by interacting with pathological proteins such as amyloid-beta and α-synuclein, creating a vicious cycle of copper dysregulation and protein aggregation. This review provides new insights into the pathophysiology of vascular endothelial dysfunction and neurodegenerative diseases by highlighting the pivotal role of cuproptosis. Understanding how cuproptosis links copper metabolism to cell death pathways opens avenues for identifying novel therapeutic targets. Interventions that restore copper homeostasis or block cuproptosis-specific molecular events may offer promising strategies for treating these devastating diseases.

papers.title: The A53T Parkinson's Disease Mouse Model Shows Abnormal Outer Retinal OCT Metabolic Biomarker Patterns.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to test for abnormal optical coherence tomography (OCT) metabolic biomarker patterns in the A53T Parkinson's disease model, which accumulates α-synuclein in photoreceptor inner segments before overt motor symptoms. METHODS: Four-to-6-month-old transgenic A53T homozygous mice and B6C3H wild-type (WT) littermate controls were evaluated using 2 OCT metabolic biomarkers. The first was the external limiting membrane (ELM) to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) thickness, a proxy for subretinal space acidification and retinoid deficiency. The second biomarker was the sub-ELM hyper-reflective band profile shape minor:major aspect ratio, a proxy for mitochondrial configuration within photoreceptor inner segments. We also tested for outer nuclear layer (ONL) thinning, OCT metabolic biomarker sensitivity to light-dark conditions, and nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (Nnt) expression. RESULTS: A53T mice showed inferior and superior subnormal ELM-RPE thickness, and a supranormal sub-ELM hyper-reflective band profile shape aspect ratio in the inferior but not the superior retina. Central retinal ONL thickness was unremarkable between groups. Compared to light, dark-adaptation evoked contraction in ELM-RPE thickness and an increase in sub-ELM hyper-reflective band profile shape aspect ratio in both cohorts. In addition, B6C3H control mice expressed functional Nnt. CONCLUSIONS: The abnormal OCT metabolic biomarker patterns raise the possibility of central outer retinal dysmetabolism in A53T mice, despite normal ONL thickness. Light-dark results show that ELM-RPE contraction can be caused by increased metabolic demand in the A53T mouse model.

papers.title: 1,8-Cineole (Eucalyptol) in Neurodegeneration: From Pharmacological Mechanisms to Therapeutic Applications.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases represent an enormous global burden, and due to the lack of effective therapies, the number of affected individuals continues to rise, placing a significant pressure on patients and their families. Phytochemicals such as terpenes are a group of compounds that have the potential to provide long-term neuroprotective effects by targeting multiple pathobiological pathways and supporting the brain's natural defense mechanisms. 1,8-cineole (eucalyptol) is a monoterpene known for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, mainly utilized in the respiratory system. However, due to its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier, beneficial effects have been observed in the central nervous system. Here we examine the pharmacological mechanisms and neuroprotective potential of 1,8-cineole in the nervous tissue. Studies have shown that 1,8-cineole has the potential to suppress neuroinflammation and reduce glial activation, activate antioxidant defense mechanisms and scavenge reactive oxygen species. Additionally, 1,8-cineole has been shown to modulate central neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity, inhibit apoptotic neuronal death and regulate ion channels involved in pain modulation. This review aims to examine the therapeutic potential of 1,8-cineole in the most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases in the population, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, as well as brain injuries, including ischemic stroke and traumatic brain injury, which may lead to neurodegeneration. We also explore the potential benefits of 1,8-cineole for anxiety and depression, which occur as early symptoms or common complications of neurodegenerative diseases. Given the need for novel therapeutic approaches, combination therapies that utilize the therapeutic potential of phytochemicals, such as 1,8-cineole, may enable more effective targeting of the multiple, interconnected pathobiological processes underlying neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Visual feedback increases expiratory muscle training effort in Parkinson's disease: a randomised crossover trial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Disorders of airway protection, including impaired cough and swallowing, are clinically important complications of Parkinson's disease. Expiratory muscle strength training (EMST) is an established non-pharmacological intervention targeting these deficits. The aim of this study was to evaluate the acute effect of visual feedback provided by the SpiroGym mHealth app on expiratory muscle activation during EMST in people with Parkinson's disease. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, randomised, two-period crossover trial in people with Parkinson's disease. Participants performed EMST under two conditions, in randomised order: conventional EMST without visual feedback and EMST with real-time visual feedback provided by the SpiroGym app. Expiratory muscle activation was measured using surface electromyography of the abdominal muscles. The primary outcome was the within-participant difference in mean peak normalised internal oblique activity between conditions. Secondary outcomes included external oblique and rectus abdominis activity, associations with neuropsychiatric symptoms, and participant-reported usability ratings. RESULTS: Twenty participants were randomised, and 19 completed the study and were included in the final analysis. No study-related adverse events occurred. Visual feedback significantly increased mean peak normalised internal oblique activity compared with no feedback (118.2 ± 36.4% vs. 90.5 ± 23.0% of reference voluntary contraction; p < 0.001; Cohen d = 0.95). Without feedback, internal oblique activation significantly declined from 100.1 ± 22.2% in the first set to 84.4 ± 25.5% in the fifth set, whereas it remained stable with feedback (120.3 ± 29.4% to 119.9 ± 40.6%). papers.title: A comprehensive review of the neurobehavioral and neurotoxic effects of 6PPD-Q in fish, rodents, and humans.
papers.abstract: N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N'-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine (6PPD) is a widely used tire additive that undergoes environmental transformation to 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q), which is ubiquitously detected in environmental matrices. Increasing evidence demonstrates that exposure to 6PPD-Q adversely affects organisms through neurobehavioral disruption and neurotoxicity. While studies document behavioral abnormalities and molecular alterations, a comprehensive synthesis linking these outcomes remains limited. The objective of this review was to synthesize current literature reporting neurobehavioral and neurotoxic effects of 6PPD-Q in fish, rodents, and humans using experimental and computational approaches. Using PRISMA guidelines, a search was conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar using several key phrases related to 6PPD-Q and neurotoxicity, capturing 1874 records. Relevant articles were assessed by full-text review for criteria eligibility, and the final review included 27 articles. In fish, exposure to 6PPD-Q can alter neurobehaviors like locomotor activity, anxiety-like responses, social and aggressive behaviors, and disturbances in circadian-regulated activities. Such behavioral outcomes correspond closely with neurotransmitter imbalance, neuroendocrine disruption, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and transcriptome changes affecting neural signaling pathways. In rodents, repeated or chronic exposure to 6PPD-Q leads to neuronal damage, cognitive impairment, anxiety-like behavior, and memory deficits. Human biomonitoring and mechanistic studies further associate 6PPD-Q exposure with oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and molecular responses relevant to neurological diseases. Leveraging the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database, computational analysis revealed entities associated with 6PPD-Q in the database were related to Alzheimer's disease, dopaminergic synapses, neurotrophin signaling pathways, and Parkinson's disease. papers.title: The ability of the commercial inertial measurement unit-based gait system in determining Parkinson's disease: A systematic review with meta-analysis of cross-sectional studies.
papers.abstract: The purpose of this study was to use the meta-analytic approach to investigate the ability of Inertial Measurement Unit-based commercial system measured gait variability and asymmetry in distinguishing individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD) from healthy controls (HC). Cross-sectional studies included using commercial IMU-based systems measuring gait variability or asymmetry at any stage of PD patients and healthy adults were included. Studies were determined by searching for four electronic databases and cross-referencing. Dual selection and data abstraction of studies were conducted. Hedges' g standardized mean difference was calculated for each variable and pooled using inverse heterogeneity mode. Statistically significant was determined by two tailed z-alpha values ≤0.05 and non-overlapping 95% CI. Heterogeneity was estimated using Q and I2 with alpha values ≤0.10 for Q considered statistically significant. Small-study effects were examined using doi plots and LFK index. A total of 1,725 studies were screened. Eventually, 9 studies representing up to 571 PD patients and 470 HC met the inclusion criteria. Overall gait variability was significantly greater in individuals with PD than in HC (Hedges' g = 0.368, 95% CI 0.139-0.597). The multi-IMU subgroup also showed significantly greater gait variability (Hedges' g = 0.397, 95% CI 0.221-0.574), whereas the one-IMU subgroup did not. However, the between-subgroup difference was not statistically significant, and the multi-IMU prediction interval included null. The primary analysis detected no statistically significant overall difference in gait asymmetry (Hedges' g = 0.180, 95% CI -0.012-0.373). These findings provide preliminary evidence of an average group-level difference in gait variability but hard to establish individual-level discrimination, clinical utility, or the superiority of multi-IMU systems.

papers.title: Assessment of change in drug-induced parkinsonism in daily-life gait using vision-based machine learning.
papers.abstract: Drug-induced parkinsonism is a potentially reversible movement disorder that may be subtle and difficult to monitor in residential dementia care. Vision-based machine learning analysis of gait may provide unobtrusive longitudinal monitoring around medication changes. We conducted a two-center cohort study of 61 residents with dementia receiving psychotropic medication. Hallway gait sequences were recorded using ceiling-mounted cameras and converted to three-dimensional body pose. A TabPFN classifier estimated UPDRS-III item 29 gait severity for each walk. We evaluated associations between acute antipsychotic (AP) and antidepressant (AD) dose reduction/cessation (≥50% dose reduction or cessation, 0-21 days after change) and daily mean predicted gait severity using linear mixed-effects models in ever-exposed participants, with complementary equal-weight paired analyses among participants observed in both medication states. In mixed-effects models, acute AP dose reduction/cessation was associated with lower predicted gait severity (β=-0.127, p = 0.022), whereas AD dose reduction/cessation was not (β=-0.060, p = 0.210). Equal-weight paired analyses found no statistically significant participant-average within-person change among paired participants (AP mean change = 0.031, 95% CI [-0.114, 0.176], p = 0.653; AD mean change =-0.021, 95% CI [-0.098, 0.056], p = 0.575), consistent with heterogeneous individual responses. Vision-based monitoring captured within-participant gait variation around psychotropic dose-reduction periods, but findings are associative. Larger prospective studies with documented reasons for medication changes are needed before using such monitoring to guide medication decisions.

papers.title: Targeting the microbiota-gut-brain axis in Alzheimer's and Parkinson´s disease: recent therapeutic approaches.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) are the most common neurodegenerative disorders with limited disease-modifying treatment options. Evidence suggests that the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA) plays a role in these diseases by facilitating communication between the gut and the central nervous system. Associations have been found between altered gut microbiota composition and function, impaired barrier integrity, dysregulated metabolite production, and immune activation to neuroinflammation and progressive neurodegeneration. AREAS COVERED: This review summarizes and critically assesses recent studies from the past year to provide an updated overview of therapeutic strategies targeting the MGBA in both diseases. We discuss dietary interventions, probiotics, postbiotics, microbial metabolites, and approaches targeting gut barrier function. We also highlight strategies such as fecal transplantation, photobiomodulation, and PD-targeted metabolism therapies using butyrate and resistant starch. EXPERT OPINION: While these interventions have shown promising results in preclinical and early clinical trials, their clinical application is limited by methodological heterogeneity, interindividual variability and a lack of standardized protocols. Successful implementation requires carefully designed clinical trials, particularly longitudinal studies of presymptomatic cohorts, standardized microbiome analyses, and integrated multi-omics approaches to elucidate causal relations and facilitate personalized treatment strategies.

papers.title: Ketogenic Diet and Neurological Health: A Narrative Review with Natural Language Processing-Assisted Thematic Mapping Using BERTopic.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The ketogenic diet (KD) is an established therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy and is increasingly investigated across other neurological disorders. OBJECTIVE: To provide an updated narrative synthesis of recent mechanistic and clinical evidence on KD across neurological disorders, including its therapeutic applications, potential mechanisms, and current evidence gaps, and to use BERTopic as a supplementary natural language processing tool to characterize major research themes and temporal changes in research emphasis. METHODS: Literature published from 2021 to early 2026 was retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed. After deduplication and eligibility screening, 1017 records were included in BERTopic analysis. PubMedBERT, UMAP, HDBSCAN, and c-TF-IDF were used for thematic mapping; interpretation and evidence synthesis remained expert-guided. Temporal analyses were restricted to 2021-2025. RESULTS: Seven thematic clusters were retained, with increased representation of gut-brain-axis-related publications after 2023. Narrative synthesis highlighted energy metabolism, mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, neurotransmitter regulation, and the gut-brain axis as major mechanistic domains. Clinical evidence was strongest for drug-resistant epilepsy, while findings for Alzheimer's disease and migraine were less mature and those for Parkinson's disease remained preliminary. CONCLUSION: KD is an established therapy for drug-resistant epilepsy and shows potential across other neurological disorders, particularly Alzheimer's disease and migraine. Its effects may involve energy metabolism, mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, neurotransmitter regulation, and the gut-brain axis. BERTopic-assisted mapping complemented the narrative synthesis by summarizing major research themes and temporal trends.

papers.title: Noninvasive brain stimulation for motor function and quality of life in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) seriously affects the motor function and quality of life of patients. Noninvasive brain stimulation (NIBS) is an effective non-pharmacological approach to improve the motor function and quality of life of PD patients, but the views about the optimal NIBS intervention remain controversial. This study aimed to compare and rank the relative efficacy of different NIBS interventions on motor function and quality of life. METHODS: Eight databases, including PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, SinoMed, CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP Database, were systematically searched from inception to 15 December 2025. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) using NIBS in PD treatment were included. Mean difference (MD) and 95 % confidence interval (95 % CI) were used as effect indicators, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Pairwise meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4, and network meta-analysis was conducted using Stata 16.0. RESULTS: A total of 45 RCTs involving 2,354 patients with PD and 17 NIBS interventions were included. For motor function assessed using the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part III (UPDRS-III), the top three interventions for short-term outcomes were cTBS-SMA (SUCRA, 91.6 %), HF-rTMS-SMA (86.6 %), and HF-rTMS-M1 (84.8 %). Compared with placebo (sham stimulation), the top-ranked cTBS-SMA significantly reduced short-term UPDRS-III scores (MD = -9.80, 95 % CI -17.55 to -2.05). For long-term UPDRS-III outcomes, the top three interventions were HF-rTMS-M1 + SMA (SUCRA, 90.4 %), HF-rTMS-SMA (83.6 %), and LF-rTMS-DLPFC (73.4 %). Compared with placebo, the top-ranked HF-rTMS-M1 + SMA significantly reduced long-term UPDRS-III scores (MD = -10.05, 95 % CI -18.67 to -1.42). papers.title: The epigenetic mechanisms mediating the long-term impacts of toxicants on brain functions and health.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in toxicoepigenetics have significantly enhanced our understanding of epigenetic modifications induced by toxicant exposures. This review synthesizes current knowledge regarding epigenetic alterations - primarily DNA methylation, histone acetylation, and miRNA perturbations - associated with common toxicants, including arsenic, lead, methylmercury, formaldehyde, α-hexabromocyclododecane, bisphenol A, and fluoxetine. While substantial evidence derives from rodent models, human studies have made crucial contributions by characterizing toxicant-specific epigenetic signatures, identifying affected genes and pathways, and establishing epigenetic regulation as a critical mediator of biologic responses. This review highlights parallels between toxicant-induced epigenetic changes and those observed in neurologic disorders, particularly focusing on the potential of epigenetic marks as early diagnostic tools for synaptic dysfunction in Alzheimer disease, but also focusing on Huntington disease and Parkinson disease. It relies on evidence ranging from exposures in vitro and in vivo (mainly in rodents) to human exposures. It also highlights parallels between toxicant-induced epigenetic changes and those observed in brain cancers. The findings underscore the therapeutic potential of targeting epigenetic mechanisms to mitigate toxicant-induced neurologic effects. We conclude by proposing a strategic framework for further advancing toxicoepigenetic research, emphasizing the creation of a centralized databank for toxicant-induced brain epigenetic alterations, the development of validated epigenetic bioassays, and the integration of functional neuroimaging. Our proposed comprehensive approach, combining genetics, toxicology, epidemiology, and environmental science, aims to inform and enhance risk assessment protocols and therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Interrogating DNA methylation associated with Lewy body pathology in a cross brain-region and multi-cohort study.
papers.abstract: Here, we conduct a large meta-analysis of DNA methylation across multiple cortical brain regions, in relation to increasing burden of Lewy body pathology. Utilizing a dataset of 1205 samples (832 unique donors), we identify 24 false discovery rate significant differentially methylated loci associated with Lewy body pathology, with loci located in UBASH3B and PTAFR, and an intergenic locus passing the genome-wide significance threshold. Ontological enrichment analysis highlights several neurologically relevant traits, including synaptic alterations. We compare methylation signatures between neurodegenerative pathologies and highlight a shared epigenetic profile across Lewy body, Alzheimer's and Huntington's diseases, although the top-ranked loci show disease specificity. Utilizing summary statistics from large-scale genome-wide association studies, we identify significant enrichment of DNA methylation differences with respect to increasing Lewy body pathology in the SNCA genomic region. We also identify specific relationships between genetic risk variants for Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's disease to methylation quantitative trait loci in the SNCA 5' region and expression of alternative transcript isoforms.
